newsitem.title: USA: "No question" that U.S. wheat crop damaged - USDA.
newsitem.headline: "No question" that U.S. wheat crop damaged - USDA.

text.p: A cold snap that swept across the Plains last weekend damaged the nation's winter wheat crop, Al Peterlin, chief meteorologist of the U.S. Agriculture Department said Monday.
But the extent of the damage won't be known for several days until farmers inspect their fields, he added.
"There's no question we have done some damage and caused some stress to the plants," Peterlin said.
A wide area stretching from northwestern Texas to Kansas was hit with temperatures in the mid-teens to upper 20s Fahrenheit, causing some damage, he said.

"Wheat is sometimes compared to a cat with nine lives. This cat fell off a cliff and we're trying to see how many of the nine lives were used up," Peterlin said. He added it could take several days to compile an estimate of the damage.
Snow cover in mid-Kansas may have protected some of the crop there, he said, but the winter wheat planted in Oklahoma was farther advanced and had no snow to protect it.
"The stage of development of the winter wheat crop was very different from Texas up to Kansas," he said.

Kansas is the nation's biggest winter wheat producing state, with an output of 255.2 million bushels in 1996. Oklahoma produced 93.1 million bushels and Texas 75.4 million bushels that year, according to Agriculture Department statistics. The nation as a whole produced 1.48 billion bushels of winter wheat in 1996.
Peterlin also said that farm fields in the Dakotas had passed through the worst of the spring weather, and that spring planting could be slightly delayed.
"It is going to be quite wet and the rivers will remain at high levels in the Dakotas," he said. "But the worst of their suffering is over."
